title: Epidemiology and Population Health
answer: Syndromic surveillance, outbreak mapping, vaccine waning, social determinants and scarce resource allocation.

children.name: Syndromic Surveillance
children.blurb: Syndromic surveillance is the near-real-time monitoring of symptom, encounter, and other pre-diagnostic data to detect unusual patterns that may signal an outbreak or public health threat.

children.name: Outbreak Mapping
children.blurb: Outbreak mapping is the practice of tracking and visualizing where infectious disease cases, exposures, and risk factors appear over time and geography.

children.name: Vaccine Waning Models
children.blurb: Vaccine waning models estimate how protection from vaccination declines over time for specific pathogens and populations.

children.name: Social Determinants of Health
children.blurb: Social determinants of health are the conditions in which people are born, grow, work, live, and age, and the wider set of forces and systems shaping daily life.

children.name: Allocating Scarce Resources
children.blurb: AI systems used to decide how limited health resources such as ICU beds, ventilators, vaccines, staff time, or drug stock are distributed across a population.

sections.body: Epidemiology and population health uses AI to find patterns in disease across groups rather than individuals. Current systems read emergency room notes, pharmacy sales, school absence records, and wastewater data to flag unusual clusters of illness. They also estimate how fast an outbreak is spreading and which neighborhoods are likely to be hit next. Some models track how immunity from vaccination fades over time using routine lab results and case counts. Others pull housing, income, and transit data to measure social determinants of health. This is operational work, not just research, with public health agencies running these tools daily.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The honest state is mixed. Syndromic surveillance works well for common seasonal viruses but often fails to catch a new pathogen early because the signals look like ordinary colds. Outbreak mapping is reliable for diseases with clear case definitions, yet it depends on testing rates and reporting delays that can distort the picture. Vaccine waning models are still uncertain because they must separate biological decline from changes in exposure and testing behavior. Social determinants models can describe disparities but cannot by themselves fix them, and they often inherit bias from incomplete address or income data. Allocating scarce resources with AI remains contested, since fairness definitions differ and no model can resolve the underlying ethical tradeoffs.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from detection to decision. Syndromic Surveillance and Outbreak Mapping are the early warning pair, with the first focused on spotting signals in messy data and the second on turning those signals into geographic pictures of spread. Vaccine Waning Models then address a specific uncertainty that affects outbreak projections, namely how long protection lasts in a population. Social Determinants of Health explains why the same outbreak does not hit all groups equally and what data can and cannot capture about that inequality. Allocating Scarce Resources sits at the end because it uses outputs from the other four pages to guide hard choices about ventilators, vaccines, or staff during a crisis. A reader would start with Syndromic Surveillance to understand detection, move to Outbreak Mapping for spread, consult Vaccine Waning Models for immunity, then Social Determinants of Health for context, and finally Allocating Scarce Resources for the decision problem.
